# Introduction

In this assignment, we will be analyzing and creating models from data in the [Seoul Bike Sharing Demand](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/560/seoul+bike+sharing+demand) data set.

## Reading the data

The first thing we'll do is create a tibble out of provided the data.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# Load the tidyverse, ggplot and save the data to a tibble
library(lubridate)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

#Create data tibble

bike_demand<-read_csv("data/SeoulBikeData.csv",locale=locale(encoding="latin1"))

```

Note that the `locale=locale(encoding="latin1")` argument (used to fix the error mentioned in the assignment document) was found on Stack Overflow, via Google.

# EDA

## Checking the Data

### 1.

Now that we have a tibble, the next thing we'll do is check to see if there are any missing data. To do that, we visually inspect all 8,760 rows of the tibble. Just kidding, we'll use the `is.na()` function to check that and then sum it by column, to see how many missing values we are dealing with.

```{r}
# Look for missing data

colSums(is.na(bike_demand))
```

Zero's across the board, which is great!

### 2.

Next up, I'll check all the columns and basic summary stats to make sure everything is making sense.

```{r}
# Look at raw tibble

bike_demand
```

Here, we see the following columns with character data: `Date`, `Seasons`, `Holiday`, and `Functioning day` and the following columns featuring numeric (double) data: `Rented Bike Count`, `Hour`, `Temperature(°C)`, `Humidity(%)`, `Wind speed (m/s)`, `Visibility (10m)`, `Dew point temperature(°C)`, `Solar Radiation (MJ/m2)`, `Rainfall(mm)`, and `Snowfall (cm)`. Of these, one might argue that `Hour` needs to should be converted because it's a time. However, it's useful to leave it as is because it's measuring the time that's elapsed since the beginning of the day.

To make sure the data themselves are reasonable, a good place to start is basic summary statistics:

```{r}
# verify the data pass the smell test

summary(bike_demand)
```

Looking closely at the numeric variables here, nothing stands out as unreasonable.

### 3.

Next up, we'll use the `lubridate` package to convert our first column to an actual date. Note that the `Date` column gives day, then month, then year.

**Note** I've changed the name of the tibble at this point, so we can call the unchanged (`bike_demand`) tibble later, if necessary.

```{r}
# Turn first columm into date data type

demand_data<-bike_demand|>
  mutate(Date = dmy(Date))

demand_data
```

Now, just to be sure nothing got messed up too badly:

```{r}
# Check for new date column missing data

sum(is.na(demand_data$Date))
```

### 4.

Next up, we'll turn the character variables in `Seasons`, `Holiday`, and `Functioning Day` into factors. To begin, I'd like to look at what character strings are showing up because, in particular, I'm not sure what `Functioning Day` is all about.

```{r}
#Retrieve observations

unique(demand_data$Seasons)

unique(demand_data$Holiday)

unique(demand_data$`Functioning Day`)
```

The strings in the first two columns make sense to me. Looking through the tibble above, I'm only seeing `Yes`, which makes me think that maybe that column is recording whether the bike being rented is functional that day. If so, it would make sense that there aren't any `No` entries, as there wouldn't have been a bike rented if it weren't functioning. Let's check to see if, in fact, there are no `No`'s.

```{r}
# Check to see if "No" exists

sum(demand_data$'Functioning Day' == "No")
```

Well, I was wrong. There are some entries where the bike wasn't functional. Looking more closely at the information provided in the link, it says `Functional Day - NoFunc(Non Functional Hours), Fun(Functional hours)`. Maybe looking at only the entries where there is a `No` there might give a clue.

```{r}
#Look more closely where Functioning Day = "No"

filter(demand_data,`Functioning Day`== "No")
```

It looks like there weren't any rentals when we had a `No` there. To confirm:

```{r}
# Confirm no rentals when Functioning Day = "No"

filter(demand_data,`Functioning Day`== "No") |> pull(`Rented Bike Count`)|>sum()
```

So, it seems like that column is registering times when someone went to rent a bike, but the bike wasn't functioning (and so nothing was rented).

With that in mind, we'll next finish what we set out to do in this problem: create factors.

```{r}
# Create levels as appropriate

demand_data <- mutate(demand_data,
  SeasonsF = factor(Seasons, levels = c("Winter", "Spring", "Summer", "Autumn")),
  HolidayF = factor(Holiday, levels = c("No Holiday", "Holiday")),
  FunctioningF = factor(`Functioning Day`, levels = c("Yes", "No"))
)

demand_data
```

### 5.

Next up, we'll rename the columns so they're a bit friendlier (and all lower case). Note that I'll rename the factorized columns with lower case (sans `F`) for simplicity and tack on `_old` to the columns we no longer want to use.

```{r}
# Rename columns

demand_data <- demand_data |>
  rename(
    date = 1, 
    bike_count = 2,
    hour = 3, 
    temp = 4, 
    humidity = 5, 
    wind_speed = 6, 
    visibility = 7, 
    dew_pt = 8, 
    solar_rad = 9, 
    rainfall = 10, 
    snowfall = 11, 
    Seasons_old = 12, 
    Holiday_old = 13, 
    Functioning_old = 14, 
    seasons = 15, 
    holiday = 16, 
    functioning = 17
  )

demand_data
  
```

### 6.

For this part, we'll create summary tables. To being, we'll do a basic summary across the numeric variables. Recall that, earlier, we noticed that the tibble records whether the bike was functioning. So, in the summary below, I'm going to subset on times when the bike was functioning.

```{r}
# Five +1 number summaries across numeric data

six_num_sum <- apply(X = demand_data |>
                       filter(functioning == "Yes")|>
                        select(where(is.numeric)),
                      MARGIN = 2, 
                      FUN = summary
                      )
six_num_sum
```

Next up, let's look at some one way tables based on categorical variables.

```{r}
# One way tables
one_way <- list(
  seasons_summary = demand_data |> group_by(seasons) |> summarize(count = n()),
  holiday_summary = demand_data |> group_by(holiday) |> summarize(count = n()),
  functioning_summary = demand_data |> group_by(functioning) |> summarize(count = n())
)

one_way
```

Next, we compare bike rental counts between functioning and nonfunctioning hours. This helps us decide which observations to retain for our analysis.

```{r}
# Summarize hourly rentals by functioning status
demand_data |>
  group_by(functioning) |>
  summarize(
    hours = n(),
    mean_rentals = mean(bike_count),
    median_rentals = median(bike_count),
    sd_rentals = sd(bike_count),
    min_rentals = min(bike_count),
    max_rentals = max(bike_count)
  )
```

Nonfunctioning hours have zero recorded rentals. We exclude these hours so that the remaining analysis describes bike rental demand while the service was functioning.

```{r}
# Retain functioning hours for the remaining analysis
demand_data <- demand_data |>
  filter(functioning == "Yes")

# Check the number of retained rows
nrow(demand_data)
```

Using the functioning hours, we next compare hourly bike rental counts across seasons.

```{r}
# Summarize hourly rentals within each season
demand_data |>
  group_by(seasons) |>
  summarize(
    hours = n(),
    mean_rentals = mean(bike_count),
    median_rentals = median(bike_count),
    sd_rentals = sd(bike_count),
    min_rentals = min(bike_count),
    max_rentals = max(bike_count)
  )
```

Summer had the highest average hourly bike rental count, at approximately 1,034 rentals, followed by autumn at 924 and spring at 746. Winter had the lowest average, at approximately 226 rentals per hour. The medians followed the same seasonal pattern. Hourly rental counts also varied more in summer, which had the largest standard deviation at approximately 690 rentals, compared with approximately 150 in winter. These summaries suggest that rental demand differs across seasons, although they do not account for other factors such as weather.

We also compare hourly rental counts between holidays and nonholidays.

```{r}
# Summarize hourly rentals by holiday status
demand_data |>
  group_by(holiday) |>
  summarize(
    hours = n(),
    mean_rentals = mean(bike_count),
    median_rentals = median(bike_count),
    sd_rentals = sd(bike_count),
    min_rentals = min(bike_count),
    max_rentals = max(bike_count)
  )
```

Nonholidays had a higher average hourly rental count than holidays: approximately 739 versus 529 rentals. The median was also higher on nonholidays, at 561 compared with 259 on holidays. Rental counts showed somewhat greater variability on nonholidays, with a standard deviation of approximately 644 compared with 574 on holidays. We compare averages rather than total rentals because the dataset contains many more functioning hours on nonholidays than on holidays. These are descriptive comparisons and do not establish that holiday status causes the difference in rental demand.

So far, each observation represents one functioning hour. Next, we will summarize the data by date, season, and holiday status so that each retained day has one observation for the remaining analysis.

### 7.

Next, we combine the hourly observations into daily summaries. We group by date, season, and holiday status, then calculate daily totals for bike rentals, rainfall, and snowfall. For the remaining weather variables, we calculate daily averages. These summaries use the functioning hours retained in the previous step.

```{r}
# Combine the retained hourly observations into daily summaries
daily_demand <- demand_data |>
  group_by(date, seasons, holiday) |>
  summarize(
    bike_count = sum(bike_count),
    rainfall = sum(rainfall),
    snowfall = sum(snowfall),
    temp = mean(temp),
    humidity = mean(humidity),
    wind_speed = mean(wind_speed),
    visibility = mean(visibility),
    dew_pt = mean(dew_pt),
    solar_rad = mean(solar_rad),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# View the daily dataset
daily_demand
```

### 8.

Now that the data have been summarized by day, we revisit the numerical summaries. The bike rental count now represents the total rentals during each day’s retained functioning hours. Rainfall and snowfall are summed across those hours, while the other weather variables represent averages.

```{r}
# Summarize the numeric variables in the daily dataset
daily_summary <- apply(
  X = daily_demand |>
    select(where(is.numeric)),
  MARGIN = 2,
  FUN = summary
)

daily_summary
```

Daily bike rental totals ranged from 977 to 36,149, with an average of approximately 17,485 and a median of 18,563. The middle 50% of daily totals fell between 6,967 and 26,285, showing substantial variation across days. Average daily temperature also varied considerably, ranging from approximately −14.7°C to 33.7°C. Rainfall and snowfall summaries contained many zeros, indicating that precipitation was absent on many of the retained days.

```{r}
# Compare the distribution of daily rentals across seasons
ggplot(
  data = daily_demand,
  mapping = aes(x = seasons, y = bike_count)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Bike Rentals by Season",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Daily Bike Rental Count"
  )
```

Daily bike rental counts differed across seasons. Summer had the highest median daily rental count, followed by autumn, spring, and winter. Winter also had the smallest spread in the middle 50% of daily counts, while spring had the largest. Summer had three unusually low daily totals, shown as points below the lower whisker. These observations may warrant closer examination, but the plot alone does not establish why they were low.

```{r}
# Explore daily rentals in relation to average temperature
ggplot(
  data = daily_demand,
  mapping = aes(x = temp, y = bike_count)
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Bike Rentals and Temperature",
    x = "Average Daily Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Daily Bike Rental Count"
  )
```

Daily bike rentals generally increased with average daily temperature, although the relationship appears curved rather than perfectly straight. Rental counts were generally highest around 20–25°C and tended to decrease at higher temperatures. There was also considerable variation among days with similar temperatures, suggesting that temperature alone does not explain daily rental demand.

Next, we examine correlations among the daily numeric variables. These describe the direction and strength of pairwise linear relationships, including relationships between bike rental counts and weather variables. We also examine correlations among the weather variables because some predictors may contain similar information.

```{r}
# Select the numeric variables from the daily dataset
daily_numeric <- daily_demand |>
  select(where(is.numeric))

# Calculate Pearson correlations
daily_correlations <- cor(daily_numeric)

# Display correlations rounded to two decimal places
round(daily_correlations, digits = 2)
```

Daily bike rental counts had positive correlations with temperature (0.75), solar radiation (0.74), and dew point temperature (0.65). Correlations with rainfall (−0.24) and snowfall (−0.27) were negative but weaker. Humidity had little linear association with rental counts (0.04), although this does not rule out a curved relationship or an association after accounting for other variables. Temperature and dew point were very strongly correlated (0.96), suggesting that these predictors contain overlapping information. Including both in a regression model may make their individual coefficients harder to interpret.

# Split the Data

We next randomly divide the daily data into approximately 75% training data and 25% test data. We stratify the split by season so that each season is represented in roughly similar proportions in both sets. The training data will be used to fit the models, and the test data will be used to compare their prediction errors. We set a random seed so that the split can be reproduced.

```{r}
# Make the random split reproducible
set.seed(558)

# Split the daily data, sampling within each season
bike_split <- rsample::initial_split(
  daily_demand,
  prop = 0.75,
  strata = seasons
)

# Extract the training and test datasets
bike_train <- rsample::training(bike_split)
bike_test <- rsample::testing(bike_split)

# Check the number of days in each dataset
nrow(bike_train)
nrow(bike_test)

# Check seasonal representation
table(bike_train$seasons)
table(bike_test$seasons)
```

The split produced 263 training observations and 90 test observations. Each season is represented in both datasets, with approximately three-quarters of its days assigned to training and the remainder assigned to testing.

# Fitting Multiple Linear Regression Models

We will use multiple linear regression to predict daily bike rental counts from weather and calendar variables. Before fitting the models, we will use the date to create a weekday/weekend factor in both datasets, then exclude the date itself as a predictor. We will also standardize the numeric weather predictors by subtracting their training-set means and dividing by their training-set standard deviations. The test predictors will be standardized using those same training-set values.

We will compare three models: one containing the specified weather and calendar predictors, a second adding the specified interactions, and a third adding squared temperature and humidity terms. Each model will be fitted using the training data and evaluated using test-set root mean squared error (RMSE), where a smaller value indicates lower prediction error. Following the assignment instructions, we will then refit the model with the lowest test RMSE using the full daily dataset and report its coefficients.

## Prepping Data for Modeling

Let's start by creating the weekday/weekend factor, using the *mutate* and *wday* functions from ***tidyverse*** and ***lubridate*** respectively. We will create a wrapper function for this process, and then apply it to both our testing and training data sets.

```{r}
day_to_weekenday <- function(df, date_col, new_col_name = "day_type"){
    df |>
    mutate("{new_col_name}" := factor(
      ifelse(wday({{date_col}}, week_start = 1) %in% c(6, 7), "weekend", "weekday"),
      levels = c("weekend", "weekday")
    ))
}

bike_train<-day_to_weekenday(bike_train,bike_train$date)
bike_test<-day_to_weekenday(bike_test,bike_test$date)
```

Next, let's standardize our variables. We'll create a function to standardize each numeric column based on the mean and standard deviation of an inputted training set, enacting the standardizing on the "test" set, but we can just input the training set as the test set to standardize it in the same way.

```{r}
standardize_variables <- function(df_test, df_train) {
  col_names <- names(df_train)
  for (col in col_names) {
    orig_col <- df_train[[col]]
    is_num <- is.numeric(orig_col)
    is_date <- inherits(orig_col, c("Date", "POSIXt"))
    if (is_num && !is_date) {
      m <- mean(orig_col, na.rm = TRUE)
      s <- sd(orig_col, na.rm = TRUE)
      if (is.na(s) || s == 0) {
        s <- 1 
      }
      df_test[[col]] <- (df_test[[col]] - m) / s
    }
  }
  return(df_test)
}
bike_train_szd<-standardize_variables(bike_train,bike_train)
bike_test_szd<-standardize_variables(bike_test,bike_train)
```

## Model 1: All Variables with no Interactions

Our first model is a standard linear model using all of our standardized numeric variables, and also our factor/categorical variables.

```{r}
model_1 <- lm(bike_count ~ seasons + holiday + day_type + rainfall + snowfall + temp + humidity + wind_speed + visibility + dew_pt + solar_rad, data = bike_train_szd)
```

## Model 2: All Variables with Limited Interactions

Our second model includes all of the previous predictors, but also interactions between seasons and holidays, seasons and temperature, and finally temperature and rainfall.

```{r}
model_2 <- lm(bike_count ~ seasons*holiday + seasons*temp + temp*rainfall + seasons + holiday + day_type + rainfall + snowfall + temp + humidity + wind_speed + visibility + dew_pt + solar_rad, data = bike_train_szd)
```

## Model 3: All Variables with Limited Interactions and Quadratic Terms

Our third and final model includes all previous terms, and adds a quadratic term for temperature and humidity using I() notation.

```{r}
model_3 <- lm(bike_count ~ seasons*holiday + seasons*temp + temp*rainfall + seasons + holiday + day_type + rainfall + snowfall + I(temp)^2 + I(humidity)^2 + wind_speed + visibility + dew_pt + solar_rad, data = bike_train_szd)
```
